utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon to everyone. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to say good afternoon to everybody present; the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, Mr. Karnavas who is back with us, and also the accused who are present here in the courtroom. As you know, today we have a witness and he will take three days. Before that, I'd like to make two oral rulings which were pending. The first relates to expert -- the expert report of William Tolsanovic [as interpreted] and General Major Pringle. On the 10th and 12th of May, 2006, the Prosecution sent in to the Chamber and Defence counsel expert -- the expert report of Mr. Tomljanovich and that of Mr. Pringle pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Defence counsel of the accused opposed the expert reports, questioning the witnesses, and they also asked to be able to cross-examine the expert witnesses. The Chamber deliberated the issue, and wishes to underline first of all that the Defence counsel did not provide any specific reasons justifying their opposition to the request made by the Prosecutor on the 10th and 12th of May. On the other hand, the Chamber wishes to observe that General Pringle has already testified as an expert witness in another case before the International Tribunal. Having read the expert reports and the curriculum vitae of the authors, the Chamber considers that William Tomljanovich is very well able to testify because he -- as an expert witness on the subjects that he deals with in his report, the organs and structure of Herceg-Bosna, and that also applies to General Pringle with respect to subjects related to military issues, as a military commander. Pursuant to a request made by the Defence, the Chamber considers that William Tomljanovich and General Pringle should testify in person before the Tribunal in order to be able to answer questions put to them by the counsel during the cross-examination. The Defence counsel will be able at that point to contest the validity and relevance of the conclusions contained in the expert reports. The Trial Chamber also wishes to observe that when these two witnesses testify and when they are cross-examined by the Defence, that on the basis of all that they will be able to decide what probative value and weight to give to their reports and testimony. Therefore, I wanted to tell you that the two expert witnesses will be appearing and the Defence teams will be able to start the cross-examination stage after which the Chamber will rule on the admissibility of the reports and the relevance and probative value of the subject matter and contents of those reports. I'm now going to ask us to go into private session, because there's another ruling that demands private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're in open session. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With respect to your -- your decision concerning expert Tomljanovich, while I don't take exception with the fact that he has a Ph.D. in history, given the content matter, given who he works for and so on and so forth, we on the Defence side - and I think I can speak for everyone regarding this issue - do not see him as an expert. Accordingly, with leave, we certainly would like to leave that -- we would like -- we would be filing some sort of a pleading expressing our collective position with respect to why Mr. Tomljanovich should not testify as an expert, but he might be competent to testify as something other than an expert. And the reason for that, Mr. President, is because obviously when it comes to giving weight, I believe in many jurisdictions, national jurisdictions, even international jurisdictions, weight is normally given more to an expert as opposed to a layperson. And I would -- I would suggest that at least the Trial Chamber ponder the suggestion that I'm making that, prior to him being designated an expert in the field in which he's going to testify, as opposed to being an expert in history, that the Prosecutor first lay a foundation and then request that he be deemed an expert by the -- by the Trial Chamber. In other words, seek the Trial Chamber's imprimatur before he testifies as an expert. That would be my request, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. We have taken note of what you have just told us. There's a decision that was rendered, on the other hand, last week, which was recorded on Friday concerning an issue -- issuance of an appeal request to a decision having to do with the co-counsel in the Alaburic team, and that decision was taken by a majority vote, and I personally had a separate opinion with respect to that decision. There was another decision taken with respect to the computer, laptops that the accused could use in the courtroom. That decision will be recorded with the Registry over the next few days. The Trial Chamber over the past few days looked into the question of our schedule for September, October, November, and December, and we decided, as we had already indeed decided at the very beginning, at the outset, to sit for just four days a week; Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. It is our assessment that the very impressive quantity of documents that are being tendered makes it incumbent upon us to read those documents, and if we don't have enough time to read the documents, we're not going to be able to do our job properly. So for that reason, as has been the case so far, we shall be sitting four days a week with just a light difference. So far we were able to work two days a week morning and afternoon. However, as the Srebrenica trial is going to go ahead, we're going to have to limit our sittings to Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday morning or afternoon, depending on the schedule that the Srebrenica Trial Chamber has. So I should like to invite the Prosecution to take that on board when it decides on its witnesses. Two months later we're going to see whether we're keeping up to schedule on time or whether we're lagging behind. For the moment we're still within the proper time limits, but if there is any lagging behind, then we will see what we can do and reassess the situation. But for the moment, everything is fine. We're all present. Nobody is ill. We're all in the courtroom so that we can all fulfil our duties and obligations and the demands of this trial. Yes, go ahead, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. For several days now I have been thinking about the tendering of exhibits of Witness Hujdur. We had to get everything in a very short space of time, so would you allow me to tender the exhibits now? I only have three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. With respect to the Hujdur exhibits, we haven't made a ruling there yet. No decision has yet been made. Everything depends on a far more general question, and that is the request made by the Prosecutor with respect to the admissibility of a number exhibits relating to the previous witness. Mr. Murphy last week also intervened, so we're going to make a ruling that is going to take into account all the exhibits, and once we render our ruling, we'll come back to Hujdur and the exhibits you wish to tender. So it's a little premature for the time being. We're putting everything on standby as everything will depend on our decision ruling.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can, of course, give us the numbers of the exhibits you'd like to have tendered, and then we'll make a definite decision in due course. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, that's just what I wanted to do. The Defence of Mr. Stojic would like to tender the following exhibits into evidence: 2D 00054, 2D 00055, and 2D 00056. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now going to turn to Mr. Scott. The incoming witness, how much time do you think you'll need? We're going to be sitting for three days this week; six hours tomorrow, six hours the day after, plus the four hours today. So we're going to devote about 16 hours to this witness, taking into consideration examination-in-chief and cross-examination. Now, how long do you think you're going to take with the examination-in-chief, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. I hope to be able to finish this witness in something around the range of six to seven hours. It is my hope that -- hopefully much better than that, but the witness sometimes has a tendency to give rather long answers, and so I'm allowing for that possibility. However, it is our goal to use the time in such a way that we should be able to finish the witness this week, allowing ample time for cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. So if you take up six hours, that leaves us with 10 hours for the Defence. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I no longer need to go to the gymnasium to keep in shape because I'm carrying documents for witnesses such as the one that's coming. These are the documents that we have to go through. They're quite -- quite a number of them. He's a critical witness. I don't want to be pessimistic, but I don't think that there will be enough time, 10 hours, for the cross-examination of this gentleman, given the scope of his -- of his testimony, because it goes to all sorts of things, especially - especially - joint criminal enterprise. I just mention this. We on this side will be extremely diligent in trying to be as efficient as possible, but I just throw that out right now. He's an extremely important witness, and of course I think we may need to bring him back if we're not finished with him. I just mention this, although I'm not saying that we can't. At this point it seems almost impossible, because, as I said, there are a lot of documents and we can't just spend 30 seconds, and we're going to try to tell a story, as the Prosecution is going to do under direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But let's not waste any more time. So without further ado, let's have the witness introduced into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're doing that, to use the time efficiently, I meant to respond and I wanted to do it to use as little time as possible, about Mr. Karnavas's comments concerning the witness Tomljanovich. Your Honour, it is the Prosecution position the Prosecution has already tendered Mr. Tomljanovich as an expert and the Court has already ruled that he is accepted as an expert. So I am not sure what it is Mr. Karnavas seems -- he wants to litigate it a second time, but as far as I'm concerned, he's been tendered as an expert, he's been accepted as an expert, and he will be presented as a live witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In just in one sentence: He is an employee. He is a bought-and-paid-for employee of the Prosecution. He's not an expert. He's not independent. He's an employee. It's like me having my co-counsel testify. That's what I mean. I'm not saying he's not competent, but he's not the same as some independent individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber has all the elements before it now. We have given an oral ruling a moment ago. We have also taken note of what you have said. We are going to discuss the matter amongst ourselves this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, would you stand, please. I'm going to ask you first of all whether you understand what I'm saying in a language you understand. If you do, please say "I understand."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have been called to testify as a witness by the Prosecution. Before you take the solemn declaration, could you tell me your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Stjepan Kljuic. I was born in Sarajevo on the 19th of December, 1939.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your present profession or your activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At present I'm a counsellor for foreign policy, advisor for foreign policy in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified before this Tribunal or another Tribunal on the events that took place in your country in 1992, 1993 or 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can you tell me quickly what cases you testified in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was called as an expert witness to confirm certain documents, authenticate certain documents in the Kordic trial, and I was a legal witness in the Milosevic and Krajisnik trials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Will you now read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to say something before I begin my testimony. [In English] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What does -- what subject is it on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I refuse to be a Prosecution witness, and I was subpoenaed to be a Court witness. So I have come here not through my own free will, but I was taken into custody and brought here. As a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I respect the decision of our state which is binding on all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina to place themselves at the disposal of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is the problem that you wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, with respect to that problem, you know that this Tribunal has been functioning for the past 10 years and is functioning according to a confrontational procedure, that is to say the Prosecution calls witnesses, and the Defence calls witnesses. That is the general principle. Now, if somebody is quoted, name comes up quoted by either of the parties, that person is obliged to come to the Tribunal. If the party calling the individual encounters a difficulty, then the Trial Chamber issues a subpoena so that that person can come into the Tribunal to testify. That is the principle of this International Tribunal, but it is also the principle applied in all international tribunals. When somebody's name is listed, they have to appear. You said a moment ago that the Trial Chamber can decide itself that it would like to hear such-and-such a witness. That is because their -- the witness comes in when there seems to be a gap. In Blaskic, for example, there were witnesses that came in following a subpoena from the Trial Chamber. In Kubura and Hadzihasanovic, there was also a witness of that kind. But as we haven't got a general view of the overall case at this stage, we didn't want to call you as a Trial Chamber witness. So therefore, you are coming as a Prosecution witness. You could have come as a Defence witness. But once you have taken the solemn declaration, you are a witness of justice. You are not a witness of either party. The fact that you have taken the solemn declaration means that you are a witness of justice, and that is what I wanted to explain to you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That is what I wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like now to give you some additional explanation. As I told you a moment ago, we are in this common law proceedings, which means that the witness first of all answers questions put to him by the Prosecution. Once the Prosecution have completed the examination-in-chief, the witness is then cross-examined by the Defence counsel, and also by the accused if they wish to ask questions. The four Judges sitting in front of you can also ask you questions during the proceedings at any time. Obviously, in a national system of continental law, it would be me who asks the questions to begin with and then the others follow. But as we're in a different system here, it is the Prosecution that starts off by asking you the questions, and then the Judges can ask for clarification when they feel necessary. The Judges can also ask you questions without going through me. The Judges are equal, so no Judge is above another Judge, so the Judges are free to ask their questions themselves and don't have to go through me. If a question seems to you be complicated, then you can ask the person asking you it to reformulate the question. The important thing is to hear what you have to say in response. The Prosecution and the Defence, when they're asking their questions, will also be showing you documents, most likely, different documents in order to see what your opinion of them is and what you know about them. You will be, of course, telling the truth. There is no question of mendacity in the Tribunal. That goes without saying. I know that you have understood this full well, how important the solemn declaration you took is. If you encounter a problem during the proceedings, please let us know. We're going to be working for an hour and a half and then take a 20-minute break, after which we shall resume for another hour and a half. So today we're going to take that break at approximately 20 to 4.00. We shall reconvene at 4.00 and have another break at about 5.00, and go on working until 7.00 p.m. As your testimony's important, you're going to be testifying for three days; Monday, Tuesday morning and afternoon, Wednesday morning and Wednesday afternoon. So that is the time envisaged for your testimony as both parties consider it to be important. It will take three days. That, in general terms, is how we're going to conduct these proceedings. As I said a moment ago, don't hesitate to let me know if you have any difficulties whatsoever. Having said that, I turn to Mr. Scott and give him the floor for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, before we start, can you once again state your full name and spell both your first and last name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to stand up or remain sitting?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You can just give us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] Stjepan Kljuic, and it's spelled S-t-j-e-p-a-n, K-l-j-u-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kljuic. I was asked to assist -- some of the recordkeepers with that. Sir, I'm going to go through some of your background to give the Judges an overview leading up to your testimony today. So I'll move through this fairly quickly. As you've already indicated, sir, I understand you were born in Sarajevo on the 19th of December, 1939.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your ethnic origin is Croat, and you consider yourself to be a Roman Catholic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You studied philosophy and literature in both Zagreb and later in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You worked for approximately 35 years as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During most of this time, perhaps all of this time you would consider, you were what you consider to be a dissident in the communist system that then existed in the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand that you were a journalist at the Sarajevo-based paper Oslobodjenje from 1964 to 1971; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then you worked for a paper called Vjesnik, which I understand to be a Zagreb-based newspaper, but you were based in Sarajevo from 1971 to 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before that, I was thrown out of Oslobodjenje. I didn't leave the Oslobodjenje office of my own free will. I was dismissed as unsuitable. The real reason was my struggle for the equality of the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: From September, 1990, to at least February of 1992, you were the president of the political party known as the HDZ, or Croatian Democratic Union, of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I should have preceded that by saying you joined the HDZ political party in 1990.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member and one of the organisers of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you served for a time as the political secretary of the party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. Political secretary and acting president.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And your time as president of the party, did that continue from approximately September, 1990, to at least February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In addition to your positions in the political party, is it correct, sir, that you were a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina from approximately the 9th of December, 1990, until the 4th of November, 1992, and again from the 24th of October, 1993, until October, 1996?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In June, 1994, you formed a political party called the Republican Party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Does that party still exist today?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It does, but for four years now I have not been active in politics. I have withdrawn from political life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us in just a couple of words, a few words, what the political philosophy or platform of that political party is, or at least was at the time that you founded the party and were active in it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It was the first attempt to create in Bosnia and Herzegovina a multinational West European party which was to reconcile the conflict between the former communists and the national parties that emerged at the first democratic elections in 1990. In the general chaos in Bosnia, its aim was to try and find a way out of that chaos. Initially the party was very well-received by the citizens, but as time went by, we received no assistance from the West, and the national parties, after the end of the aggression in Bosnia-Herzegovina, grew ever stronger and are still in power in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, with that background in mind, I'd like to go back to some of these things in considerably more detail in some respects. In terms of -- you said a moment ago that you were not only a member but a founder of the political party HDZ-BiH. Can you tell us again briefly what you did in terms of assisting in organising or establishing that party?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The first political parties on the territory of the former Yugoslavia were established in Slovenia and Croatia. This was the route democratisation took, from the west towards the east. There came a time when, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, political parties were founded. Some of them, such as the Party of Democratic Action, which was the first to be founded, did not reveal their ethnic and religious identity in their title, but according to their platform and their membership, it was an exclusively Muslim party. As the Croatian Democratic Union had been founded in Zagreb and won at the elections, it was quite natural for the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina to establish our own party on that political basis. We had a lot of assistance from the people in Zagreb, because once democratisation took hold in the former Yugoslavia, the Croatian emigres population, the Croatian diaspora, provided enormous funds which all went to Zagreb and helped them to win the election. Zagreb then took on the task of assisting the founding of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, you should know that the situation was very complicated. After 45 years of totalitarian regime, all of a sudden parties can be founded, and various ideas cropped up. Zagreb had a list of people. Some of them had arrived from abroad, and some citizens from Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted to become involved. I have to say that the first problem that arose was what the status of the party would be, whether it would be a branch of the Croatian HDZ from Zagreb and whether it would be called the HDZ for Bosnia and Herzegovina or whether it would be an autochthonous Bosnian Herzegovinian party of Croat origin called the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course, I was in favour of it being an independent political party, the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that's where major problem arose, when the party convention was held in Sarajevo on the 18th of August, 1990. During the preparations, I was at the head of a significant group of intellectuals from Sarajevo, but we were not given the appropriate importance, and the president of the coordinating committee was Mr. Davor Perinovic. During the preparations for the party convention, there was some very dramatic situations, because the Croatian Prime Minister - Croatia had already established its own government - arrived in Sarajevo. But on the 17th of August, in the evening, there was an incident in Knin. On that day, the Serbs in Knin set up barricades and started causing incidents all over Croatia. The Croatian police set off in helicopters intending for the police forces of the Republic of Croatia to calm down the situation. However, the JNA, with its aircraft, neutralised the helicopters and forced them to land. That night in Knin, there was an armed rebellion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to come back, please, to the question of the formation of the party. And the convention that you've indicated existed -- the convention that was held on the 18th of August, 1990, did you attend that convention?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you've indicated that a number of officials, or at least you mentioned the Prime Minister, that some people from Zagreb, from the Croatian government or party in Zagreb, came to the convention. Can you tell us who those people were, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, I tried to explain to you that Mr. Manolic arrived, but when the incident in Knin occurred, as he had come on the plane belonging to the Republic of Croatia, Sarajevo airport was empty, but a truck hit his plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apart from Mr. Manolic, who were the other people who came from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: There were Dalibor Brozovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who he was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: He is a member of the academy. He was born in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He is a prominent Croatian person, active in culture. Then there was Gojko Susak, minister from the emigres community, and the general secretary of the HDZ, Miljenko Zagar. There were very many people from abroad, very many people from our municipalities, from Neum to Brcko, municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Croats from Sarajevo among whom were the intellectuals who were candidates for the leadership of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, why it was that the senior officials of either the Croatian government or the Croatian party the HDZ, why they were in attendance at the convention in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It's quite simple: They wanted to help us, to help us create a party which would be in political harmony with the HDZ in Zagreb. You should know that at that time the national interests of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the national interests of the Croats in Croatia were more or less identical. The idea was to create a democratic Yugoslavia with more autonomy for the republics based on the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the convention on the 18th of August, 1990, you mentioned a Mr. Perinovic, I believe. Mr. Perinovic was elected as president of the party, Mr. Davor Perinovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. Davor Perinovic and his people, because he submitted a list of his people, including -- well, it was a very heterogenous list. Most of these people were not familiar with the real situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they were very hard-line, demanding things that were not appropriate at the time in that political situation. Therefore, I, as the leader of the group of intellectuals from Sarajevo - and none of these people I was the leader of - entered the leadership of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, to use your terminology, sir, what were some of the "very hard-line demanding things," that you say Mr. Perinovic's group made?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: One can see that from the speeches held before the convention itself. There was a rally held in Prozor, several speeches made to the Sarajevo press, and I have to say that the Croats in Sarajevo found these speeches hair raising, and they refused to become members of the HDZ at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: They were hair raising in what way?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, for example, Mr. Perinovic said that the Muslims were actually Croats of the Islamic faith, that Croatia should extend as far as the River Drina. Well, you'd have to find this in the documents, but these were terrible statements and made at a time when the regime was still a communist one. And this did not correspond with the real political aspirations of the Croatian people and, moreover, were not realistic at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who was it that selected or named Mr. Perinovic to be a candidate for president and then indeed elected president? Who was behind him?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, some 10 days previously they had established a steering committee which included the representatives of some municipalities and Mr. Perinovic, and of course they had the support of the HDZ from Zagreb. The main man at that time was the Secretary-General, Miljenko Zagar, who was in constant communication the night before with our group and with Perinovic's group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's go forward, and I think some of these other things will come up again as the chronology unfolds, sir. At the convention on the 18th of August, 1990, is it correct that the party also adopted a written statute or constitution?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was envisioned. The atmosphere was very heated. An agenda was adopted, a statute, rules, the conditions for membership, but all this was done in purely formal terms and there was political discussion among the representatives of various regions, and a document was finally adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With the registry's assistance, could I have the witness shown Exhibit 13 -- well, P 00013.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you're able to look at that document, and it may be that you may want the ushers to assist you if you want to page through the document a bit. When you've had a chance to look at that document, sir, could you tell us -- could you confirm that that is the statute of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina as adopted on the 18th of August, 1990?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I had such a document in my hands because all those attending the convention were given a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And does this appear to you, sir, to be a copy of that same document?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Could you go back to Articles 3 and 4, please. And could you zoom in a bit, please. It seems to be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, you've mentioned some issues concerning Mr. Perinovic. Was he then removed a short time -- a few days later, a short time after the convention, as president of the party?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, it's at least been commonly reported that the reason -- or one of the reasons that Mr. Perinovic was removed was because he was found in fact to be at least part -- in part a Serb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: There was mention of that, but that was not the chief reason for his dismissal, his Serb origin. A woman who was a member of the HDZ brought his baptismal certificate from Bileca, showing that he was a Serb actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you tell us, then, how you became named acting president in this situation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Before the founding, I had been a candidate, first for political secretary and later on, when some people gave up, I assumed the duty of political secretary and acting president. When on the 17th of August, in the evening, our demands were not adopted, I broke off negotiations and left. As I was leaving, Milenko Zagar, the general secretary, asked me whether this was my final word. I said yes. And I said, "Sooner or later, you'll come knocking on my door."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's jump, sir, to about the 5th or 6th of September, 1990. Did you have occasion to be travelling through Zagreb about that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And tell us what happened at that time.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I was approached by some people who said, "Come with us." When I got into a Buick, on the back right-hand seat, I said, "Gentlemen, it's quite clear we're not going to the Petrinjska police station." After a while, they brought me to President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, excuse me. I wonder whether all this information came out during the proofing session, because I don't believe we received any proofing notes, and this seems to be rather new material. So if we could have some -- a clarification on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My understanding, it's in previous statements of this witness, including his testimony in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I should note, Your Honour, that we only have one statement, one prior statement. Which reminds me, as I understand, during the Kordic case when the gentleman testified, he indicated that he had given a statement which had not been provided to the Defence. Also, I should note, in the Kordic case again, Mr. Nice was reading from some sort of a summary, again as I understand, it's not part of the EDS and we don't have it. So I don't want to disrupt the flow of the direct examination, but perhaps at the break the Prosecution could be so kind as to provide us that material. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As far as I know, Your Honour, there is no additional material to be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is the Prosecutor then conceding the point that there was no statement given by this gentleman prior to his testimony in Kordic? Because that's what the gentleman testified to under oath, and I can provide the page number to the Trial Chamber if necessary. We don't have that statement. We have one statement that the gentleman gave in the year 2000. I'm simply asking the Trial Chamber to instruct the Prosecutor to perhaps look and see whether there was an oversight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll make further inquiries, Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, what do you have to say to that? I have the impression that you are -- that you are examining on the basis of a statement provided by the witness in the Kordic trial, and this is a statement not provided to the Defence, if I understand correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Your Honour, to clarify, I am examining from my own private outline, which has nothing to do with the witness. It's something I prepared for purposes of my examination. As to the other -- whether there is other statements by this witness, I'll certainly make further inquiry. Indeed he's testified in three other cases, as he's indicated to this Chamber a few minutes ago, in the Kordic case, in the Krajisnik case, and in the Milosevic case, and he has given extensive evidence and information in these cases. But the short answer is, Your Honour, I'll make further inquiry. If there is indeed anything that should be disclosed, then it will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So when you went to see -- when you were taken to see President Tudjman, what happened at that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Quite simply, he asked me whether I would work for our cause. I said, "General, I have been doing that for 30 years." He then talked to me about how I might agree to lead the Croatian Community of Bosnia-Herzegovina [as interpreted]. As I was a professional journalist, at the time working for a German radio station broadcasting in our language and I had signed an agreement with the German government, I was duty-bound to spend 10 days in Germany presenting the leaders of the parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina to our citizens living and working in Germany. In the meantime, a meeting was held in Zagreb of all the municipal representatives of the organisations of the HDZ and the leadership of the Zagreb HDZ, and they decided that I should take over the role of president. I learned about this while I was in Frankfurt. After that, we arrived in Sarajevo, and on the 16th of September, the Main Board of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which had this authority under the statute, appointed me acting president.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I want to go back to page 27 of the transcript, line 4. I don't know if it was a translation or transcription error perhaps or perhaps you misspoke. It says in reference to President Tudjman, it says, "He then talked to me about how I might agree to lead the Croatian Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Did you mean to say the Croatian Democratic Union or HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I said the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's a political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. So you returned to Sarajevo. On the 16th of September there was a meeting of the Main Board; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you were named acting president at that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have -- ask that the witness please be shown Exhibit P 09617. For Your Honours, that will be in the second -- that particular document will be in the second bundle. Most of them will be pretty much in the order of the bundle, but that one is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I missed the first part of that document, sir, but have you seen enough of that document? Can you tell us, please, is that a record of the meeting on the 16th of September, 1990, indicating the fact that you were named acting party -- excuse me, acting president of the party at that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did the party also elect vice-presidents and a secretary at that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you recall, can you tell us, who were the three persons elected as vice-presidents on the 16th of September, 1990?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: One of them was Ante Bakovic, the other Nikola Krizanac, and I can't recall who the third was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The third person Abid Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was -- he had been vice-president with Perinovic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was he a person of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim, but he represented himself as a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Ignac Kostroman was elected as secretary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I was the general secretary. He was the business secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just make one clarification. The Prosecutor indicated that on this particular day the Main Board met. From the document it's rather clear that it was not the Main Board but the Executive Board. Perhaps the gentleman could verify that for the record, and then perhaps he could give us a distinction if there is one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, if you could look at the top of the document and correctly identify the party -- excuse me, the part of the party, the board, or function or apparatus of the party that met on that day that puts you in this position.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's quite clear that this is the Executive Board. The Main Board was in Zagreb. The Main Board is a broader body. The Executive Board is a more narrow body of leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't like interrupting, but when you read this sentence in line 15, it would appear -- when he says the Main Board was in Zagreb, he said in the context of the Croatian language that the meeting was in Zagreb, not the Main Board, whereas this can be interpreted as saying that the Main Board was in Zagreb. He meant the meeting of the Main Board was in Zagreb, the session. So if we could clear that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you for explaining that to us, Counsel Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I want to make sure that it's your testimony. If there's anything about what's been said in the last few minutes that you want to clarify, please do so; otherwise, we will go forward.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: We can go forward, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but while I was speaking and when the -- you intervened, he said yes, the session was in Zagreb. I can't see that in the record. It must be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sir, could you confirm that the session took place in Zagreb so that we have that on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The meeting of the Main Board of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina was held in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That has been recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you -- can the registry please next show the witness Exhibit 15, or P 00015.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, is this a -- the records of a meeting of a session of the Presidency, the Executive Board, and members of the Municipal Board of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina meeting on the 8th of October, 1990?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you have a delegation attending this meeting from Zagreb, including Mr. Susak?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the general business conducted at this meeting, if you can just briefly describe it to us?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that it was just before the elections, and we were supposed to organise a massive participation in the voting of our workers abroad. And since Mr. Susak was the minister for persons abroad of the government of Croatia, we didn't want to make a parallel project. What we wanted to do was, via this ministry, we wanted to inform and involve as many of our nationals to vote in the Bosnia-Herzegovina elections that were held on the 18th of November and 4th of December, 1990. The communist press gave large-scale publicity to Verinovic [as interpreted], and there was no reason to do that except as a political diversion. When I was appointed on the 16th of September, the very next day I asked that the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina be registered as a party under my presidency, and the court accepted that registration, thereby rejecting any complaints by Perinovic. But in the press several days after that, there were many of his statements in which he disclosed some of his conflicts he had had with Zagreb and with certain individuals from Zagreb. And at that meeting, and we had the Municipal Board of Sarajevo represented, we expected that we would have large-scale support. However, there were these local leaders who had to prepare for the elections, and you must know that the atmosphere that prevailed at the time was highly tense throughout Yugoslavia. People quite simply after having 45 years of a one-party system were not ready and did not believe that the time had indeed come for part -- several parties to appear, and they didn't know who to vote for, who to choose, because very few people believed at the time that the communists would lose the elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at the last page of Exhibit P 00015, and can you just look at the list of names associated with various positions on that document and just tell us if that appears to you to be an accurate listing of the officers and members of the Presidency of the party at that time.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, except for the fact that from Tomislavgrad the base hadn't delegated anybody for the Presidency. I was from Sarajevo, Nikola Krizanovic was from Bugojno, Ante Bakovic was from Gorazde, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: There should have been regional representation, and that's why we had one seat reserved for Tomislavgrad, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Then, sir, directing your attention to elections in November and December, 1990, is it correct that there were two rounds of voting? There was a first round on the 18th of November and a second round on the 4th of December, 1990 -- 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that of the Croat candidates who were running for office at that time you received the most votes, with approximately 33 per cent of the vote?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you remember, can you tell the Judges, in that election, how many seats in parliament did the HDZ BiH win or obtain?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: We obtained 44 seats in parliament, in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it had a total of 240 seats, and we won two seats in the Presidency representing the Croatian people. That's as many as we could have had. And we also won a large number of the municipal seats, municipal presidents, amongst whom in 10 towns in which the Croats were not the majority population. In fact, in nine of those towns they were second. In Kotor Varos, they were the third ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of the two seats that the party won on the Presidency, who took those two seats?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I came first, and Franjo Boras came second.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To what, sir, did you -- do you attribute the success of the HDZ party in the 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, first and foremost, we compiled a national programme, and I made that public. Perhaps there was some Croats who had done that before me, but because of the political depression during communism, they were not able to publish it in the country. So that political programme of mine can be summarised in very simple terms: It was for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, equality for the Croatian people within it, and five points which were designed to enable the Croats to be successful in life and co-existence in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those five points were as follows: That we had the most numerous diaspora of all the Bosnian-Herzegovinian peoples; that we had alongside us the Republic of Croatia that we could cooperate with on an economic level and so on; that we had great economic support -- great support by the Pope, who strove to have a just delineation in Yugoslavia; and that we had the largest number of literate people, which is not negligible in Bosnia-Herzegovina; and the main point was that the Croatian citizens had in their hands one -- in 1990, 70 per cent of the foreign currency capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And you have to know that the dinar was not convertible currency and that foreign exchange was bought and that the overall financial potential of the citizens, 70 per cent of it was in the hands of the Croats, which is an enormous economic advantage. So on the basis of that and on our firm resolve to have the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina be identical to Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia and other republics and equality, we won the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask that the witness next be shown Exhibit P 00022.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you have a chance to look at that document, sir, can you tell the Judges whether that is a party programme that you assisted in preparing this particular document dated the 9th of January, 1991.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Now, did you go about then to organise a party convention? Not a meeting simply of the Executive Board or the Presidency but a convention of the party that was held in Mostar on the 23rd and 24th of March, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: After the victory at the elections and the party's success and my own personal success, I was still the acting person because an HDZ convention hadn't taken place yet. So as a legalist, I wanted us to hold the regular convention as soon as possible, the party convention, in which would elect the party bodies and functionaries in view of the fact that certain people had become very prominent during the pre-electoral campaign and scored good results. And of that provisional party that was formed and which acted under those conditions, we had to turn it into a real political organisation over a four-year period to create and set up the bodies and organs which would allow the functionaries to perform their duties as best as possible. That means an economic council had to be set up, cultural cooperation council, a council to look into social welfare and health, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. To give the Judges some idea of the mix of the party, the geographic mix of the party, is it correct, sir, that approximately -- there were approximately 288 party representatives at the convention? Of that 288, approximately 53 came from Herzegovina? Sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how many delegates there were, and that's how many were from Herzegovina. And in creating our party, we inherited the communist recipe, according to which the leadership had regional representation. That is to say, from all the regions there were representatives. And the ratio was 83 per cent of the representatives were from Bosnia, and 17 per cent from Herzegovina. But we didn't insist upon that drastic difference, because at that time we did not want to divide Croats into whether they were from Bosnia or whether they were from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us once again, as in the previous meeting, were -- was there a delegation of senior officials from Zagreb at this meeting or convention?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall the names of any of the individuals who attended on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. Among others, there was Mr. Gojko Susak, but at that convention there were representatives of many other parties. It was the power and authority, the HDZ was the ruling party, and we had a large number of delegates who came to address our convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I look at the time, and I'm going to start another question or two that will go into a different area. This might be a time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's 20 to 4. We're going to break and resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I'd like to ask you a few questions about a man named Mate Boban, whose name I don't think has come up yet in your testimony. You made reference to the convention -- the opening of the founding Assembly, if you will, excuse me, the founding Assembly of the HDZ BiH party in August of 1990, and you've also mentioned the 1990 elections that were held, which resulted in your election to parliament and to the Presidency. At either the founding Assembly or during the 1990 elections, was Mate Boban a participant in either of those events, as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: As for the creation of the HDZ in -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo on the 18th of August, he was not. But he was at the elections as one of the candidates for the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he was elected among 44 representatives of the HDZ in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did he represent any particular geographic area or constituency?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, he was elected for the Mostar constituency, where the HDZ won 12 seats, 12 representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you went to the party convention in March of 1991 that we were talking about before the break, you ran for president of the party and a number of other persons also ran; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Boban was one of the other persons who ran for president at that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us the result in -- if you recall, the number of votes that Mr. Boban received in contrast to the number of votes that you received?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Boban received 32, Miljenko Brkic 1, Miro Lasic 1, and I secured all the rest; I think about 230, 240 votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You out-paced Mr. Boban quite considerably; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Despite that, was Mr. Boban elected to any office or position in the party at that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was the second vice-president, mine, and the first was Vitomir Lukic, the writer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can have the assistance of the usher to show you Exhibit 31, P 00031. As soon as you have that, sir, can you look at that enough to sufficiently tell the Chamber, if you can, whether that is the political platform of the HDZ BiH party as adopted on the 23rd of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Could you zoom down -- yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you in particular think that there was a need for having a written political platform or party platform at this time, or was it just primarily a matter of routine party business?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, in the turbulent times, it's difficult to unite the political party from the leadership down to the last member, from top to bottom. But stylised in this way, a political programme stylised in this way was the succous of what was most important and what was united at that convention as a party programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward from the convention, sir, something that will come up, I believe, in the course of your evidence, can you tell the Judges about something called the Helsinki Agreement of 1975 and how that entered into your philosophy and thinking as to the condition or constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Precisely because of the sudden political changes on the territory of the former Yugoslavia that were taking place in all the political parties, a large number of people appeared without any political education. The Helsinki Conference, which was held in 1974 in Helsinki, was the key document for the future of Europe. At the time, as you already know, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, the OSCE, was formed, and one of the most important principles that the Helsinki Conference brought was that there can be no forcible change of borders in Europe, which guaranteed the stability of political life on the old continent. And this was to be a very important point when we came to explain our politics and policies and also to our rivals and parties, other political parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because even before the elections, rumours went round according to which the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not a certain one. What happened was that many Serb politicians in Bosnia-Herzegovina, first and foremost Biljana Plavsic, said that Bosnia-Herzegovina was a Yugoslavia in small, and all the demands made from Slovenia, Croatia, and later Bosnia-Herzegovina, who wanted to gain their independence, especially as interpreted by the Badinter Commission, according to which the Yugoslav constitution, the 1974 Yugoslavia constitution, was recognised as the valid constitution, and it claimed that the republics, through their will, united to form Yugoslavia, many people ignored the Helsinki Conference. I insisted upon that point, and as it turned out ultimately, the decisions of the Badinter Commission were accepted and all the republics of the former Yugoslavia gained their independence, but the decision of the Badinter Commission was taken in 1991, whereas Montenegro gave up that independence but it, too, is independent today. So that was a political prerequisite, saying that no destruction of Bosnia-Herzegovina could be discussed; all that could be discussed was the internal set-up and system for the country. And in addition to that, Bosnia-Herzegovina is an old state which has had unchanged borders since 1669 and the Karlovac Peace Treaty. And when it lost its independence in 1463, it came under Turkish occupation and was a separate administrative entity under the Turks too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to go forward at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just be allowed to finish, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt, but there's something which is strange. You said -- that's what the record says on line 5 of page 40, that Bosnia-Herzegovina had the same borders since 1669. And then you said "... when it lost its independence in 1463 ..." One expects a later date. But is that what you wanted to say, that the borders are the same since 16 -- since the 17th century?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] '99. That was the Karlovac Peace Treaty, '99. And I also wanted to say that when it was under Turkey, it was a separate administrative unit. When it was under Austro-Hungarian occupation, it was also a separate unit entitled "corpus separatum" until the dictatorship of King Aleksandar in 1929 it was also a separate administrative unit. The only time it was not that was from 1929 to 1941. In communist Yugoslavia, Bosnia and Herzegovina was a republic on an equal footing with all the other republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The 1975 Helsinki Agreement, was that signed by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry there's still an unclarity. The witness on the first and second lines of his previous statement, lines 19, 20, speaks of '99. Which -- which century?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1699, the Karlovac Peace Treaty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the 1975 Helsinki Agreement was signed by President Tito at the time when Yugoslavia was still a combined state?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The American president Ford, the Soviet president Brezhnev, Josip Broz Tito, and 29 other statesmen from Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, we're up to March of 1991, having discussed the party convention. Did you hear around this time or become aware of meetings between Franjo Tudjman and Slobodan Milosevic at a place called Karadjordjevo on or about the 27th of March?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When was the first time that you recall learning about that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The first time I heard about that for certain is in a book written by Mr. Sarinic, who for a while was the Prime Minister of the Republic of Croatia. This book was published some seven or eight years ago in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall previously discussing the topic with Stipe Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: There were rumours going around both on the Serb side and the Croatian side, as well as the Bosnian side in Sarajevo, to the effect that there was some kind of secret agreement, but nobody said anything specific about it. Even in the most intimate conversations President Tudjman never mentioned Karadjordjevo to me or said anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you and your political colleagues observe any difference, any apparent difference in President Tudjman's views towards Bosnia-Herzegovina before and after -- after this rumoured meeting in Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It was evident that there was to be a certain change in Croatian policy requiring more agreement with the Serbs. But for us this was unacceptable for several reasons. One reason was that the Serbs were already shelling Vukovar and Dubrovnik in Croatia, that in Bosnia-Herzegovina they were separating off territories, and not just those where the Serb population was in the majority. With the help of the JNA, they were embarking on a project called Ram. I was the first person to publish the information about the Ram project, listening to secret conversations between Milosevic and Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before you get too far ahead, can I just go back to earlier in your answer. You said it was evident there was to be a certain change in Croatian policy, requiring more agreement with the Serbs. On lines 9 and 10, and you said, "But for us this was unacceptable." Who is the "us" that you referred to at that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I'm referring primarily to the leadership of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina but also to the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Continue on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may interject here. If you look at the question and look at the answer that was just referenced to earlier, the gentleman hasn't quite answered the question whether before and after the alleged meeting in Karadjordjevo. And I guess what I don't want is an unclear record. So is his answer in regard to that specific question or is he talking about because of the events as they were unfolding, ultimately the Croats were going to have to recalibrate their policy?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, before it leaves the page, I think the question and answer are exactly as they say on the page, and the witness was giving a specific answer to my question, did you observe a difference in policies before and after Karadjordjevo, and the witness gave a responsive answer, we submit: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you then talked about --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, do you confirm that after Karadjordjevo you observed a difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't clear right away, but as events developed, relations between certain Croatian politicians and certain Serb politicians grew closer and closer at more than one level. Later on, we got evidence that this was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were talking -- you began to talk about something called Ram - Ram or Ram, I'm sorry - R-a-m. Can you continue on that, please, but again, please be reasonably concise.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: As in the then Yugoslavia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, everybody was listening to everybody else. The Serbs had the institutions of the army and the police, and I obtained certain information in various ways, and very often, in exchange for payments of money, I was able to listen in to conversations between Milosevic and Karadzic. In one such conversation, they joked about this and said, "A man like Ramo." "Ramo" is a Muslim name in Bosnia, but when you listen to the tape more than once, you understand that they're talking about Ram, R-a-m, which was to encompass the old idea of a Greater Serbia as far as Karlobag, Karlovac, and Virovitica. I made this public, and there are documents showing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's go forward in terms of the HDZ BiH in Bosnia and Herzegovina during this time. Mr. Kljuic, as an overview of matters that we'll talk about in more detail in the next few hours, can you tell the Judges, over the course of 1991, from the convention forward, was there an increasing political division between at least two factions in the party that is the HDZ BiH?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: First, you have to understand the context in which all this was happening. In the spring of 1991, there was an armed conflict in Croatia. By that time, the Serbs had blocked one-third of Croatian territory, but from Easter 1991 onwards, from the incident at the Plitvice Lakes and several days after that when 12 regular Croatian policemen were killed in Borovo Selo, there was an escalation of hostilities. All this had repercussions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the initial successes of the Serbs in Croatia encouraged Karadzic and his satellites in Bosnia-Herzegovina to raise tensions. At that time, many volunteers from Bosnia and Herzegovina went to the war theatre in Croatia, and reservists from Serbia and Montenegro arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The last hopes that the Yugoslav leaders would agree on the reconstruction of Yugoslavia fell through. The situation was also confused because the American Secretary of State, Baker, in late March, 1991, said that it was in America's strategic interest to preserve Yugoslavia. After that, Milosevic stepped up the pressure on the republics. In the meantime, he had united Serbia by force, because he replaced the representatives of Vojvodina and Kosovo, the two provinces, in the Presidency of Yugoslavia, Mr. Sapundzija and Krunic, and installed his own men. In that way --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I'm going to stop you there and go back to my original question, please. Can you tell the Judges, over the course of 1991, was there a split in the HDZ BiH political party with you representing -- primarily representing one faction and Mr. Boban representing the other faction?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Not yet. Not in the first half of 1991. There was no evident split at that time, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell the Judges, then, please, when you first saw this split developing, the first manifestation of a division in the party involving you and Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Boban, as a person, was not a natural leader. He was a second-rate leader. He never opposed me in public. However, when links were severed with Zagreb, and communications, and it was not possible to communicate, only from the western parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which were not within the Serb SAO Krajinas, could one easily reach Zagreb. In this respect, this was not official Croatian policy. It was individuals in Zagreb representing certain functionaries who originated from Bosnia-Herzegovina and who showed a lot of will to make the decisions about what was to be done instead of the established leadership of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo and the political office-holders in Sarajevo. I insisted with President Tudjman that he should not receive those people, that they should come to Sarajevo and then we would see what the problem was. But the development of the military situation in Croatia, the atrocities that followed, as well as the fact that communications were blocked in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that those people in Zagreb continued making suggestions and issuing directives, certain people in the field took less and less notice of the decisions we were making in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you, in just a few sentences, to tell the Judges -- to describe the political, the official political position of the HDZ party at this time under your leadership and your political views. I want you to describe those, and then I'll ask you to describe the views of this other faction. Please tell the Judges your political and the party's political views at that time.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: First of all, I succeeded in my political programme, for which I gained the undivided support of the citizens and the HDZ members at the convention in Mostar. And to be quite clear, I stated all this in public. It was the task of the Croats to fight for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina and for the equal status of the Croats within Bosnia-Herzegovina in relation to the Serbs, Bosniaks, and others. This was the political platform founded, inter alia, on the Helsinki Conference. I did not believe or want to believe that Bosnia-Herzegovina could be destroyed. However, events on the ground took a different course. There were even some agreements, because when the Serbs were unable to come to any kind of agreement with me, and Mr. Karadzic had offered me 5 million to leave Izetbegovic, to abandoned him, I said to him I don't belong to Izetbegovic, I am for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the fact that Izetbegovic is saying he's in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina, well, why don't you say the same thing and there will be no problems. However, many people who are on the ground who are politically illiterate failed to understand the situation. You see, the Muslims, the Bosniaks, were as much threatened by Milosevic as we were. I felt that they were our political friends in defence, and I did something very important when I did not allow the Muslims to go over to Milosevic's side. Had this happened, the Yugoslav army, which had weapons and officers, would have mobilised hundreds of thousands of Muslims who would have overrun at least a part of Croatia. Our joint resistance caused the greatest problems for Milosevic and Karadzic. However, rumours began to go around that I was inferior to Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. There is something that has struck me in what you have said. You have said, "I did not allow the Muslims to go over to Milosevic's side." How is it that the Muslims would ask for your permission to do something like that? Perhaps you could explain, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Nobody was asking for permission, but at the top of the Muslim party I explained to many people what it would mean if they were to support Milosevic. And there were several such offers. I couldn't do this all by myself without the Muslim leadership, but it was very significant at a time when Croatia was attacked, was under attack, that the Muslims should be at least neutral. And this was a very difficult and complex task. I cannot tell you all the details now. And it was perhaps with God's help that we had the Muslims as political friends and allies. How things would develop, that's something else. But when Croatia was burning, it was very important for the Muslims to be made neutral. However, for those people who were from the provinces and who were opposed to me, it was very easy to say that I was inferior to Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you and go back to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, if that question's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said a few moments ago, when I asked you to describe your position, you said you were for -- and we've lost it on the page, but I believe an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. What was your view and the view of the political leadership of the HDZ about the sovereignty and indivisibility of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Absolutely the same. It's in all our documents. It's even in the documents published in October and November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to change gears now, sir. And again we're going to go through a number of particular events, but as an overview, what was the views of Mr. Boban and those around him in contrast to the views you've just described to the Judges in the last few minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask for some precision with the question itself. The previous question asked about the leadership. The gentleman indicated that Boban was the vice-president. So obviously from that answer I can only understand that Boban was in agreement with the gentleman with respect to his earlier answer. So if we could have time and place, if there was a split, at what period, perhaps it might be easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
