utterances.text: Sir, what was the political views of Mr. Boban and those around him if they were in contrast to yours? Then once you've told us that, tell us when this emerged or became more known to you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: First of all, we were acting as the Presidency, and every communique was approved by every member of the Presidency before it was made public. There was no opposition there. Secondly, Boban did have the support of certain municipal leaders but not all of them. On the contrary. The most prominent persons in Herzegovina at that time toed the HDZ party line, including the late Damjan Vlasic [Realtime transcript read in error "Demirovic"] who was the president of the Mostar HDZ, Milivoj Gagro, the mayor of Mostar, and many others. The influence of Mate Boban was to grow only later on, when there was a complete break in communication. He was liked in Zagreb, but officially, until the Plenary Session in February, 1992, I had no problems with Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a moment, sir, and I'll let you continue in and moment, but before we get too far ahead --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: May I interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for His Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I will start again. I would like to ask the witness when he actually referred to the persons, most prominent persons, as he put it, that at the same time they toed the HDZ party line, including the late, I believe, Demirovic, who was the president of the HDZ, Milivoj Gagro, the mayor of Mostar, and others. Does he mean that that party line was the one which was explained previously by you and the party line was the one which you professed that it was your own party line? Or do you mean the HDZ, I mean not only within Bosnia-Herzegovina? So I would like you to clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, this was officially the standpoint of the HDZ of Croatia, but above all it was the political orientation of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina and my personal political orientation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And my question, the one that I interrupted you to ask, was very similar to Judge Prandler's question, and again so the record is clear, so when you make references to persons like Zijad Demirovic and Mr. Gagro, do we understand correctly then that those persons were persons which followed this policy of a multi-ethnic, independent, sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: First of all, there's an error in the transcript. There's no Demirovic. I never mentioned any Demirovic. He keeps turning up here. I spoke about Damjan Vlasic and Milivoj Gagro. There were others. There was Nikola Mandic, the oldest deputy, and many others. We were not taking sides then, but later on, as time passed, everyone went his own way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me come back to -- we tried to start this several times. Can you then describe the views that Mr. Boban began to espouse and how they compared to the -- to your views and the people such as Mr. Gagro's.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I have to say that Mate Boban never expressed his political standpoints in public, but it was evident that with individuals from the Muslim and Serb parties, the SD [as interpreted] and the SDS, he had very close relations with them. At that time, Karadzic was looking for anyone with whom he could topple the policy of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Serb propaganda, both in Belgrade and Zagreb, constantly published news items saying that I was Izetbegovic's man. And this had an effect on people who were ignorant of the real situation. However, for the overall political situation, it was very important for the SDA not to join Milosevic, and later on when Milosevic tried the same with another Muslim leader and achieve a historical agreement --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you, please. Did the division between you and Mr. Boban become worse as 1991 went forward, and did there come a time when you were forced out of the party?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand Mr. Scott's difficulty, but I would appreciate that he would not ask leading questions of the witness on issues that are as important as the question that he just asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Also, I would supplement a couple of matters. One, on line 18 of the previous page, 51, the gentleman indicated SDA and the SDS, where Mate Boban had close relations. That's what I heard. It's not reflected on the record. Also, I believe we deserve an answer, a full answer to the last question. He was about to name, I hope, the Muslim leader that supposedly was in contact with the SDS or Milosevic to cut a deal. So I think that would help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, if you'd like to finish your last answer, the one that counsel's referred to, please do so. Then I would like to move forward, specifically forward in the chronology of 1991.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The Muslim leader's name was Alija Izetbegovic, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did there come a time, sir, when you were forced out of the party?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Perhaps -- sorry, but perhaps Mr. Scott did not hear my previous objection. This is a very important issue. It is not proper to ask leading questions in examination-in-chief on substantive issues of this kind. To the extent that that's done, it destroys the probative value of the evidence because effectively Mr. Scott is testifying instead of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, yes, try not to ask leading questions. It's the witness who ought to clarify what happened and tell us what happened without you leading him to the answers. What is interesting for the Judges - I speak for myself but I'm sure my colleagues share my opinion - is to know why, between him and Mate Boban, there is going to be apparently a divergence of views, difference of views. So that's the interesting point as far as we're concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I couldn't agree with you more, and I've been asking Mr. Kljuic for about the past 15 minutes to give us that answer, and maybe with the Court's encouragement Mr. Kljuic could answer that question. What was the nature of the division or the split between he and Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could answer that question specifically.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The parting of ways cannot be seen with the naked eye, nor was it apparent immediately. A belief in an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina became very difficult for many people in view of the situation on the ground. However, what was essential both for Boban and myself was that the party documents and programme were such as I interpreted them to be. He never opposed me, either in our private lives or at meetings. The respect people had for him in Zagreb, people in power positions, not necessarily political figures, but that grew. On the other hand, I was preoccupied with state affairs as a member of the Presidency, negotiations with the international community, and the problems that we were facing in the institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And you must realise that it was only six months after the government had changed. We were doing our best to replace communist cadres occupying leadership positions. The HDZ didn't have a computer, for instance, where the lists -- where the names of candidates would be listed and in order of value. Everybody wanted their own representatives from Zenica, Livno, and so on and so forth. Everyone wanted to get a place in the state administration. And while I was doing that kind of work, other people were sitting down and deliberating, thinking, that it wouldn't be a bad idea if the Serbs take their portion, we Croats could take -- seize our portion. But that was to culminate on the 2nd of February, 1992. And a moment ago mention was made of the fact that I was thrown out of the HDZ. Nobody expelled me from the HDZ. On the 2nd of February, 1992, I tendered my resignation and, according to the statute, I should have stayed on up until the new convention. The new convention was never held. They appointed a new man, and that was that. That was their affair. However, there -- a stream appeared amongst the Croatian leadership which was expressly opposed to the Muslims, and one of them, one of those protagonists, told me on the 2nd of February, 1992, when we parted ways -- he delivered a speech and then we parted ways. He said that the Croats would not, just because of Stjepan Kljuic, remain under the Turks for another 500 years. Perhaps it's unimportant, but rumour had it that his wife was the daughter of a Serbian intelligence agent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who made the -- sorry, sir. Who made the statement to you --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I'm a gentleman. Don't make me name names. I'm not accusing him. Perhaps he is not politically well-versed, but I told you about the incident and it's a true one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then I'd ask that it be stricken from the record. If he's not going to be mentioning names, then how can we give it any validity at some point? It's more prejudicial than probative. So either there is a retraction or there's a naming of people. I think it's very, very important for the gentleman to give us as many details and names as possible so we can verify and bring those individuals here if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will indeed ask follow-up questions to this, but I think Mr. Karnavas's position is over-extreme. I do not think it's a basis to strike the witness's evidence if he doesn't give it. I would like him to, and I will ask him further if he will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I understand correctly, on page 54, at line 22, you said, "... one of those protagonists, told me on the 2nd of February, 1992 -- when we parted ways. He delivered a speech and then we parted ways. He said the Croats would not, just because of Stjepan Kljuic, remain under the Turks for another 500 years." I'm asking you please, if you would, tell us and the Judges who that person was.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Don't make me do that, please. Defence -- well, I have my own code of conduct. I have come here to explain the situation to you, not to be exposed to things like that. The person occupies a position today, and it's not up to me to see who -- where somebody's wife comes from. I just said -- tried to explain the environment that they had come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm only waiting for the translation, French translation. Now I would like to say that in my considered view it is indeed we cannot oblige the witness to say -- to actually tell us that name if he doesn't want to. I believe that anyway the reference to that statement of that colleague of his doesn't have, so far at least, a probative value. On the other hand, the -- that characterisation of the 500 years under Turkish occupation, et cetera, is a very important one, and I would like to keep it in the transcript. So really I believe that we should be aware of the rights of the witnesses in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir, just to move forward then, and again we'll come back to this, then you resigned from the party on approximately the 2nd of February, 1992. We can understand that, correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly right. On the 2nd of February precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, with the usher's assistance can I direct your attention to Exhibit P 00032. And when you have had a chance to look at that, sir, can you just confirm, is this a written extract of the meeting of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina HDZ on the 4th of April, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Could you move the text down? Scroll down, please. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And looking at -- under -- if you'll find item 5 of the agenda simply as a reference point. And down below that there are references to the members of the Presidency, and there's a list of names, and can you just confirm that that's an accurate list of the officers of the party or -- excuse me, of the Presidency of the party at that time? It may be necessary to --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I can't see any list here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, all right. It will be necessary to go to the next page of the B/C/S version. If you can go to page 2 -- I think we may have skipped a page, unfortunately. Page 2 of the B/C/S document. All right. There, you can see, sir, if you look at the names --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. This is an exact list of the Presidency members after the convention in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I next refer you to Exhibit -- with the registry's assistance, Exhibit P 00034. Can you confirm to us, please, that this is the excerpt of the minutes of the second session of the Presidency of HDZ BiH on the 16th of April, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, a couple of questions. On item 3 -- find item 3 in the document. The items are numbered, and it should be several pages into the B/C/S version. Page 4 of the B/C/S version, item 3. In the -- in the third paragraph of item 3, it says: "We condemn any attempts to change the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Did that continue to be the official policy of the HDZ BiH at this time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this refers to the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then if you go to the last item in -- last paragraph in item 3, or, to state it differently, the item immediately above item 4, does it say: "Full support is given to the BH government in its attempts to preserve the integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina"? And can you confirm to us, please, did that continue to be the official position of the HDZ BiH as of April of 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to Exhibit 36. When you've had a chance to look at that, sir, can you confirm that these are minutes of the 3rd regular session of the Presidency of the HDZ BiH on the 29th of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this particular meeting, in the first item under the introduction, it says that this session was chaired by Mr. Boban. The registry may need to scroll down a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could you scroll down, please, for me, too, so I can see?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Apparently we're having some technical difficulties. When you have a chance, sir, could you just confirm that those are the minutes of the meeting on the 29th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on this particular occasion Mr. Boban chaired this meeting in your absence. If you can look at the document and tell us whether that is indicated.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What type of contacts were you continuing -- or were you having with the HDZ party officials in Zagreb during this time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Correct and proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how often were you meeting? Was there a -- was there any sort of system of regular meetings by which either a delegation would go from Bosnia on a regular basis or, conversely, a delegation from Zagreb would come to meet with you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The contacts were regular, at least once a week. Most often our people went to Zagreb and conveyed our positions and held consultations and then returned with suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, on the times -- in the exchange between the party in Bosnia and the party in Zagreb, who were the people from the Zagreb party who were most regularly involved in these meetings?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: There were a number of such people. When we were in Zagreb, we were compulsorily received by President Tudjman, usually also the Prime Minister Greguric, but when they came to Bosnia, there were more people. Sometimes there were high-ranking officials, other times lower down officials, which more or less conveyed what they were told in Zagreb. They didn't have their own suggestions except they might have said something on a private level, but officially speaking, they weren't of that capacity that they could give us suggestions. They just conveyed the suggestions made by others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention to the 13th of June of 1991. Can you tell the Judges, if you recall, did you and other representatives of the Bosnian party meet in Zagreb on that day?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: From the 13th to the 20th of June, two Bosnian-Herzegovinian Croatian delegations were received in Zagreb. I was on the one that was there on the 13th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall who was involved in this meeting, again on the side of Zagreb, if you will, on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Many municipal presidents, deputies, government members. There were very many people, and there are written records or minutes from that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Who of the senior either party or government officials from Zagreb attended the meeting on the 13th of June, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: There was President Tudjman, Mr. Manolic, Mr. Mesic. I'm not quite sure about Milan Ramljak or Brozovic, but there were some people from the top echelons of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall the particular agenda or purpose of that particular meeting, sir, what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the details. It's been a long time since then. But the topical situation was discussed, the current affairs. Croatia had already been well attacked. A large amount of territory had been blocked. There was the Serb -- Knin Serb uprising. And at the level of Yugoslavia [Realtime transcript read in error "Herzegovina"] amongst the presidents of the Republic [Realtime transcript read in error "public"], they were not on the road to a good agreement. And in June, the United States of America changed their position on Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in the midst of these events, sir, can you tell us what was specifically discussed, as best you can recall, at this meeting between the political officials in Zagreb and those of you coming from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose we analysed the political situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: In the lines, I believe, 18, 19, and 20, there is a sentence that when the witness said, "And amongst --" and I quote: "And amongst the level of Herzegovina amongst the Republic, they --" excuse me, "... amongst the public, they were not on the road to a good agreement." End of citation. Now it may be a question of translation. I do not understand that sentence, and at least in the interpretation I heard about - I may be wrong - that the witness spoke about the Republic of Herzegovina or probably he said Republic of Herzegovina. So I wonder if that sentence could be clarified by the witness about Herzegovina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, can you assist Judge Prandler on that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, if you start my sentence off, I didn't mention the Republic of Herzegovina anywhere. Could you start the sentence off for me and I'll be able to finish it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you said a large amount of -- I'm looking at lines 17 and 18 on page 60: "A large amount of territory had been blocked. There was the Serb -- the Knin Serb uprising, and at the level of Herzegovina amongst the public --" I'm simply reading the transcript -- "they were not on the road to a good agreement." So perhaps you can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you, because after the Serbs uprising in Knin, the rest of the context is not logical.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they said the presidents of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my recollection, the witness said that Yugoslav leaders were not on the road to reach an agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's the right meaning because the Serbs launched the uprising in Croatia. In the meantime, meetings were held of the Yugoslav republican leaders who were not able to find a solution, and the situation grew more complex because the Presidency of Yugoslavia wasn't functioning properly at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At this meeting, sir, was the position or policy of the HDZ, both in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the position or policy toward Bosnia and Herzegovina itself, was that discussed, what that position or policy should be?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there were no changes from our standpoints. We're talking about the 13th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Without talking about changes, can you tell us what the discussion was at that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The situation was very difficult. Yugoslavia's destiny wasn't known. Mr. Mesic was supposed to become president of the Yugoslav state Presidency. Milosevic didn't allow that to happen. There was an interregnum in the Presidency. On the other hand, we on the ground encountered great problems concerning mobilisation. The Yugoslav People's Army asked that young men be mobilised into the army and go to the battlefront in Croatia. People wouldn't let their children go. And this gave rise to a problem. People hid their children. They sent them abroad, and soldiers were already coming back in coffins from the theatre in Slovenia and Croatia. We had rallies organised by mothers, women, and also the Bosnian Serbs insisted that young men go and join up. So the situation was a highly confusing one. We already had refugees. So that working meeting was to see how we could help Croatia in any given situation and how Croatia could help us, but there was no discussion about a general political line. That was still very stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was there a discussion at that time of three possibilities concerning Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. I understand we're trying to save time. He can ask an open-ended question. We're leading too much. This is very critical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, we'll move on. If you don't recall any further discussion about Bosnia-Herzegovina and you can't remember, we'll simply move on.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell you that Bosnia-Herzegovina was always an integral republic and on a footing of equality with the rest of the Croatian people, but at that time it was said what we are going to do if Bosnia-Herzegovina didn't exist? And it was Yugoslavia's existence that was questioned, because at the time calls for a confederation burgeoned instead of having a centralised Yugoslavia. So these were all major issues. And now you can't conceive of a situation where political representatives of nations in the two republics don't discuss all the variants and options. But this was not binding. There's the platform. The platform existed and the Executive Board of the HDZ held a meeting and they always referred to an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croats being on a footing of equality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir. You said on line 24 and 25 the discussion of all the variants and options. And that's my question to you: What variants and options were discussed? Whether they were binding or not, what variants and options were discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It was a political analysis of the situation and prognosis. We had the situation in which the Serbs were rebelling in Croatia and were blocking a third of Croatia. We had the situation in which in Bosnia-Herzegovina certain areas were preparing to secede as Serbian Krajinas. There was a linkage of Knin and Drvar, the blocking of road communications, the failure of negotiations at the Yugoslav level, and demands to see what we would do in a specific situation, because there were fears that the fighting would spread from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina. You must never forget that some of the operations in Croatia were launched from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Not by the legal forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina devoted to the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because we didn't have an army of our own. This was done by Milosevic and Kadijevic's forces which were using the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina where the Serbs were in the majority, where they had armed them, to shell Croatia. All this was a topic of talks. And you know how it is when someone in your family's killed. People say, "I can never go together with them again." So we constantly had to calm things down, prevent the extremists from coming to the fore. One had to be patient. One had to take welfare -- the welfare situation into account, because food was running out, medicines were running out. So we had to engage the Red Cross and the Caritas to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, may I step in here. The Prosecution asked you a question. It was a very precise one. It is at line 6 of page 64, and the question was what the variants and options were during the discussion. You're a man of politics. If there are options, that means that there are some people who would like to see one set of formulas and other people others. So what the Judges would be interested in would be learning what the variants and options were that you envisaged, whereas you're answering the question very extensively highlighting all the problems that existed at the time. That's another thing. But what we're interested in now is what the variants and options were to deal with the problems. And what was your particular option. That's what we're interested in. We're interested in learning why at a given point in time you separated from Mate Boban. So in political terms, what were the variants and options on the table which envisaged such-and-such a solution or another solution? So what we're interested in -- in is in your solution, if you had one, or didn't you have one? Could you answer that, please, very specifically and precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. First of all, I wish to correct you. I was not separated from Mate Boban. I was a legitimately elected representative of the Croatian people. I had won the elections and the convention of the HDZ in Mostar in March, 1991. Secondly, it's correct that there were different talks in Zagreb, but this has to be put into the context of the situation we were in. The fundamental issue was still whether Yugoslavia was to become a federation or a centralist state. At that time, nobody believed it would break up. On the other hand, the same applied to Bosnia and Herzegovina. The political programme was that it should be sovereign and independent, but there were also people asking what would happen if Bosnia-Herzegovina disintegrated. This was all normal in any analysis of the political situation. I always firmly took the standpoint that Bosnia and Herzegovina, like all the other republics, should remain and have the same status as the others, especially after the decisions issued by the Badinter Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, was that the only option or variant discussed at the meeting, the one you just said, that Bosnia-Herzegovina should remain a sovereign and independent state? Was that the only option or variant discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, I've just told you that there was more than one option, more than one variant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Describe them to us, then, please, and who supported which.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the variants which would become topical later on was for the Croats and Muslims to join up with the Republic of Croatia. Another was that the Serbs should take what is theirs, the Muslims what is theirs, and the Croats what is theirs. These, however, were not serious programmes or analyses, they were just hypotheses put forward in the situation which prevailed at the time when there were tensions in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the situation in Yugoslavia was what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But that particular option, you said there were Croats and Muslims who wanted to join up with Croatia. Who was at the head of that concept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This all took place in private conversations. No party ever officially announced any official suggestion proposing any other option except for Karadzic saying we remain within Yugoslavia whatever it was like. However, people were coming to realise that after all the horrors of war, a compromise should be reached and a new formula devised. All the talk about the break-up of Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was something that occurred daily, but it had no political weight, and it was not the official opinion of any political representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With the registry's assistance, if we could show the witness Exhibit P 00041.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can look at that document, sir, long enough to familiarise yourself with it. Can you tell us whether these are the minutes of a meeting of the Presidency of the party, the HDZ BiH, on the 10th of July, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And directing your attention to -- in item number 1, about halfway through item number 1 there is paragraph that begins with the words, "The Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina ..."

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it goes on to say, "It will not allow BH to remain in Rump Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And we -- I think, for the record, we can agree, is BH Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us a bit more about what was being discussed around this time, by July of 1991, about allowing BH to remain in Rump Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: As you know, at that time Croatia and Slovenia had already changed their standpoints and were no longer seeking a confederation of Yugoslavia but were instead seeking international recognition and secession. In that respect, it was important for Milosevic to take Bosnia-Herzegovina, because those were their ambitions, and to create a Greater Serbia. I must say that the Croatian people did not want at any cost to remain within a Rump Yugoslavia in which the Serbs and Serb policies would dominate. Absolutely. The SDA party crucially also rejected Bosnia-Herzegovina remaining within a Rump Yugoslavia, and the SDS insisted with Karadzic, Krajisnik, and Plavsic that they should remain in Yugoslavia if they wanted but we should leave. Western Herzegovina was monolithically inhabited by Croats, but in my talks with Milosevic in Belgrade, I had a problem explaining to him what Western Herzegovina encompassed. At that point in time, we were active politically in the following direction: If Slovenia and Croatia left Yugoslavia, we would leave too. Later on, the European Union tasked us with holding a referendum, and these were correct political standpoints, as it later transpired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, in your answer just now, you made reference to talking with Mr. Milosevic about Western Herzegovina. Can you tell us the context and approximate time period in which you discussed this with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It was probably on the day when I was not chairing the HDZ Executive Board, when I was away on a trip. This was during the regular meetings of the political leaderships of Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina in Belgrade. After a vehement discussion with Milosevic, Trifunovic, and Unkovic, we told them that Bosnia and Herzegovina had to have the same status as the other republics. During lunch, Milosevic made me sit at his right-hand side, and after a few whiskeys he asked me to step to one side. He said, "Stjepan, we have a great deal of understanding for the wishes of the Croatian people in Western Herzegovina." He said -- well, I said to him, "President, we don't understand each other as to what Western Herzegovina is." Then he put his arm around me and said, "Stjepan, tell me. Half of Mostar, 70 per cent of Capljina, Neum Ljubuski, Posusje, Grude, 70 per cent of Tomislavgrad, 70 per cent of Livno, Siroki Brijeg, Citluk, and all of Prozor." I laughed at that because Prozor was a cult place in Bosnia-Herzegovina where our first kingdom was established, and there had never been a Serb there except for one policeman who couldn't find a wife, and he left and went home. So I said to Mr. Milosevic, What about Stolac? What about Mostar? What about Capljina, and so on? And he said, "That's Serbia." And I said to him, "And you want Western Herzegovina to join up with Croatia?" And he said yes. And then I showed him a Bosnian coat of arms, and that is something we do in the Balkans which I don't want to explain to Their Honours as I didn't want to explain it in the Milosevic case either, because I told the Judge there, please don't go into that, Your Honour, what matters is that Mr. Milosevic and I understand one another. They were all trying to find political partners for splitting up Yugoslavia according to a Serb formula. Only those people who believed in the Helsinki Conference, and I can say all these years later that they were right because Serbia has been left on its own and all this could have been done in 1991 without a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can just ask one clarifying question, Your Honour. Sir, you just said a moment ago, you said in line 24 of page 69, you started -- or line 25: 70 per cent of Mostar, half Ljubuski, Posusje, Grude, 70 per cent of Tomislavgrad, 70 per cent of Livno, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, no, please, please. I want to repeat this. I've been living with this all these years and I know it off by heart. Half of Mostar, 70 per cent of Capljina, Neum, Ljubuski, Posusje, Grude, 70 per cent of Tomislavgrad, 70 per cent of Livno, Citluk, Siroki Brijeg, and all of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question to you in regard to that grouping of territories was, was the proposal that someone would get that particular set of territory?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Milosevic wanted this, and he kept offering it to us Croats. For us it was a Trojan horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll leave it there, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's 5.30. We're going to take a 20-minute break and reconvene at 10 to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to move forward, but I suppose your last answer begs some clarification. You said before the break, "Milosevic wanted this and he kept offering it to us Croats. For us it was a Trojan horse." When you say "offering it to us Croats," do you say offering the territories you described on page 70 at lines 20 continuing on to page 71, line 2?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I'll be glad to do that. As you know, Milosevic knew about the Helsinki Conference, and if Western Herzegovina were to join Croatia by agreement and everything else remain in Yugoslavia, that change of borders would be possible. However, at that time, and I believe still today, nobody among the Bosnian-Herzegovinian Croats could have accepted such a solution. On the other hand, as Karadzic was unable to reach any agreement with me, Milosevic, who was a charming man, thought that he could do it perhaps. And thirdly, after that meeting rumours continued to spread about me as a Muslim quisling, which is not true, of course, nor did they ask me to obey them, nor did -- was I the kind of person who would be obedient. But it was an attempt to drag Bosnia-Herzegovina into a Rump Yugoslavia. Of course, no one at the time was able to accept such a thing, especially I as someone advocating the integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask the registry to please show you Exhibit P 00042. And can you tell us, sir, is this the records of a meeting of the Travnik region on the 21st of July, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us what this meant on the document when it says "Travnik region." Can you explain that to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The HDZ was constituted in such a way that it has a president, vice-presidents, a general secretary, a Main Board as the most important party body, an Executive Board consisting of a smaller number of people implementing the policies, and municipal boards. Every municipality, depending on the size of the membership and the number of Croats, had its own board. As the situation became evermore difficult and communications impossible and some political ideas were now expressed more openly, regions were established. Five or six regions were established, some of which never actually came to life legally. For us in the leadership, that was a good thing on the one hand, because general directives, information about the situation and about global political issues would no longer have to be conveyed to 50 or 60 municipal boards but to several regions. And then, within the region, every leadership would forward these messages and opinions to the municipal boards. But you should know that we had HDZ boards in places where the Croats were not in power nor were they in the majority. At a later stage, the composition of these regions will probably be presented and you will see that people put places in there where there were perhaps 5 per cent Croats. But the Travnik region was a central region in Bosnia where the Croats have a long-standing tradition and a significant proportion of the population. And we had had good election results there. They first elected their leadership and later held regular meetings at which it very soon transpired that they were deviating from the general political line, that they were presenting very extremist demands, and I have to say that this was quite normal if you take into consideration the people who were there, their political experience, their education, their ambitions, because this was a turbulent time when anonymous people from the former regime suddenly became political leaders. The atmosphere in all of Yugoslavia, and especially Bosnia-Herzegovina, was very difficult, and many people thought that the stronger the rhetoric the more important and significant they would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you confirm, please, was Dario Kordic the head of this regional grouping?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. Was elected by the representatives of those seven or eight municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And directing your attention to paragraph number 4, under "Conclusions," this body on the 21st of July, 1991, ordered you to call a session of the HDZ BiH Main Board. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I think that a session was planned earlier and they knew about it. And secondly, Dario Kordic could not issue an order to me for several reasons, both personal and official ones. I was his president, not he mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you understand that there was some conflict between what was perceived to be your position and the position of Mr. Kordic and perhaps some of these others as of July, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Of course, but they were minor representatives. He was a man from Busovaca. Please don't misunderstand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: But that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question was about did you understand there was some conflict between your position and the position of Mr. Kordic at this time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that was not primary at the time. I had so many problems and conflicts elsewhere that the fact that someone from Busovaca, which was a backwater, was opposing writing a letter, that was just a minor problem like, you know, if you're going to work and it's raining and you forgot your umbrella.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The question was asked whether the witness did in fact call that hearing, and that question was not answered. Could I have an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly, but I think that meeting had been scheduled before this gentleman from the Travnik region asked for it. But if you look at the agenda of the session, you'll see that what he was asking to be put on the agenda wasn't on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, what did he want to put on -- I tried to ask you what the conflict was. What did Mr. Kordic want to put on the agenda that was not on the agenda of the subsequent meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, then we would have to go back to point 4 where he says that I should be told to convene a meeting of the Main Board and to invite the leaders of the HZ of Zagreb to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, did Mr. Kordic ever tell you why he thought it was necessary to invite the people from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. In point 6 you have an explanation of what he was asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me go back to my question, directing you to paragraph 17. There's a reference there to something called a Croatian Regional Union. Can you tell the Judges whether that -- is that still some other body besides the Travnik region?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I didn't want to intervene before, but on several occasions in response to Mr. Scott's question Mr. Kljuic isn't being allowed to give a full answer. If the Prosecution deems them to be important questions, then the witness must be allowed to answer. And Mr. Kljuic was going to expound on point 6 when he was interrupted. I think they should allow the witness to complete his answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just simply trying to live within the time commitments that we made to the Chamber, and if we can't do that, then I don't know whether we'll finish within six or seven hours or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you answer with respect to paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can see clearly the position of Yugoslavia at that time. There was an aggression against Slovenia and Croatia, and all the troops that were withdrawn from Slovenia were brought to Bosnia, and Serb and Montenegrin reservists were also brought into Bosnia, and with a difficult situation of that kind Kordic puts conditions and says if the SDA wishes to remain in Rump Yugoslavia, we Croats do not. And I have to tell you that we're talking about very small provincial ambitions here that have no stronghold anywhere, either politically or with respect to status, and especially not that this be solved on an ad hoc basis from one day to the next, especially as the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic at that time, went as an observer to attend a session of the Islamic Conference of the Afro-Asian countries. And today Bosnia-Herzegovina is an observer in that body, and we saw no danger coming from there. If somebody was able to help us retain Bosnia-Herzegovina's independence, that would be a good thing regardless of the fact that that assistance later on took the wrong turn -- took a wrong turn. So in a situation of this kind, a man appears who is asking us to clear all this up. Of course it was easy for him. He didn't know the situation very well nor did he have any political responsibility as an HDZ man and as a member of the Yugoslav state Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps with that further answer we can go back again to paragraph 17. Was there something that existed at this time in Bosnia-Herzegovina called the Croatian Regional Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Not yet, but there will be with the establishment of the Travnik region, the Herzegovina region, the Sarajevo, Posavska, Bihacka, and so on regions. However those regions were to act differently. The Bihac region never actually took on a life of its own. In Sarajevo there would never be any important decisions taken, and ultimately, it was just the three regions; Posavska, Travnicka and Zapadno Herzegovacko, or Western Herzegovinian region that were to become influential.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, among those three regions, did any of those regions ever combine into something called the Croatian Regional Union?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: That was later on, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you exactly. I can't give you an exact date. But at any rate, it was either in August or September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In paragraph 13 of the document, sir, did you agree that HDZ deputies in the reference there, the sentence above references parliament and members of parliament have become puppets of the SDA policies? Did you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: What I can tell you is this: With 44 deputies, representatives, we were not able to vote on anything, carry a vote. We had to wage a policy of support to the side with better results. Now, if somebody were to consider that I, with 44 deputies, could go out and say we're going to vote on this today when there are 196 other deputies who needn't share our opinions, and most of them never shared our opinions, so that wasn't possible. And saying that our deputies were puppets is the fruit of immature politics and lack of respect for facts, and thirdly, a complete lack of understanding about how parliament worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask the witness to look at Exhibit P 00044. Can you confirm, sir, in looking at that document whether that is a -- the minutes -- excuse me, those are the minutes of a meeting of the Presidency of the HDZ BiH on the 31st of July, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the -- items -- or some of the items aren't numbered, so it's a bit difficult to refer you, but on page 2, if you can find a paragraph in which Mr. Udovicic, Markesic, and Cosic are mentioned. Perhaps you can see those names. If you can look at that paragraph for a moment. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that was about and does that relate to this proposal about regional -- some further regional organisations, and was that concept being pursued by the HDZ BiH Presidency at this time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I have to say that the first vice-president, Vitomir Lukic, died during that period of time, and I was attending -- I was on a state trip. I don't remember whether I was in Vienna or Bonn, but I was absent. So the meeting was chaired by Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And looking at the paragraph I just directed your attention to and also the paragraph second one down from that, "At its meeting the main board must analyse the possibility of the regional integration of other predominant Croatian municipalities." Is a result of these minutes that the Presidency was pursuing the further regional organisation of the Croatian HDZ communities?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I wasn't at the meeting, but they were proposing that a commission composed of Udovicic, Markesic, and Cosic look into the proposals of the Travnik region, so there's still not the force for that to be adopted. This commission didn't make any major recommendations to the project. These were very serious people. However, afterwards, the Herzegovina region linked up with the Travnik region as well as others, and it was their proposal that even in places where the Croats were in a minority, boards should be established to link up with those regions. To my mind, that was the introduction of a parastate administration. However, that process was not to evolve very quickly. Several months were to elapse until legally within the frameworks of those regions they created the necessary prerequisites for creating a united region.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to go to the next page of the document, you'll find the reference to the person you mentioned a moment ago; that's Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Under item 4 you'll see now.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Five. Ah, yes, 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You indicated a moment ago that Mr. Lukic died around this time and you see then at this point Mr. Boban was elevated to the level of first vice-president. And did that in fact happen?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, since Mr. Boban was the second vice-president and the first vice-president died, he moved up into first place and then the representative of the Bihac region, Mr. Vlado Santic, was appointed instead of Boban as the second vice-president, whereas Mr. Lukic in the government, he was the minister for religious affairs, he was replaced by Dr. Milenko Brkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Several paragraphs below that in item number 5, it talks about the procedure to appoint Bruno Stojic to the post of general manager of post and telephone service or organisation. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why would the political party have to approve Mr. Stojic going into that position? Was that a political party function?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was: In dividing up the ruling parties, SDS, HDZ, and SDA, in addition to the electoral results which dominated in the Assembly bodies and the Presidency, we also composed a government in which each party had a certain representative with the various departments. However, since at that time we still had the communist system in the economy, large state companies of importance financially, politically and so on, and important for employment, were equally distributed between three ruling parties so that the Croats, among other things, were given the pension fund, pension and invalid fund, and the PTT, the post office. These were two major projects employing many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but I have to intervene at this point. I don't think that the answer to this question will mean anything to us unless the witness is allowed to answer how people were elected generally and what the politics were. I should like the witness to be allowed to answer that and then he can go ahead and answer the Prosecutor's next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Sir, can you give us additional information about the nomination of those general managers or directors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We had a cadres commission where we had Ivan Markesic, Jerko Doko, and Mariofil Ljubic. They were members of that commission. And it was charged to gather data about all the candidates from the field, because many people from the municipalities wanted to be a part of the executive power, and that commission nominated Mr. Bruno Stojic as director of the PTT, which is the largest company -- one of the largest companies which fell to the HDZ. But that was just a proposal, whereas the government had the right to choose one out of a number of candidates, to select down, but to see that there is -- was ethnic parity. So for the railways we had somebody -- people for the railways, and then Bruno Stojic was proposed too. But this was never implemented because many people decided that he occupied an important financial position in the police force. I can't go into explanations now why that was so, but it dragged on. The whole thing dragged on. He was proposed by the cadres commission, but he was never appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can go on, please, to Exhibit P 00047. Can you tell us, sir, if these are the minutes of a meeting of the Main Board of the HDZ BiH on the 6th of August, 1991, in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you chair this meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the bottom -- much of the first page is dedicated to who was present or not present at this meeting, and in several lines down the page it says, "The absence of the following invited members is excused." One of those persons again is Mr. Bruno Stojic. Do you recall why he had been invited to this particular meeting, or can you tell us what his position in the party was at that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Very simple. He was not specially invited, but this was a session of the Main Board and high-ranking officials from the state administration had to attend, which were appointed by the HDZ or represented the HDZ, all the government ministers were invited, both members of the Presidency, assistant ministers, deputy ministers, and pursuant to his post as assistant minister I think for financial affairs or something like that, or material resources or whatever it was called, Mr. Stojic was invited to attend. So it was a routine matter, not up to me or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to item 11 of the document. Just for the record, is that a further confirmation that around this time Mr. Boban was appointed its first vice-president?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. This is a routine matter. Boban went up from two to one. Vlado Santic was mentioned as the second vice-president, and then there was a seat free. And we put Mr. Barac there, a prominent physician from Zenica, to fill in from that region. That was purely routine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look next at paragraph 21, item 21. Can you tell the Judges how this notion of the regional organisations was continuing to develop at this time. It appears to indicate that in a meeting that you chaired, the proposal was passed.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you see, this need for better linkage, better communication, meaning information, organisation of defence, and so on, required greater subordination among the Croatian leadership. Of course the first important point was to link up the regions, and then within the regions each particular place, which accelerated and simplified procedure from the top of the party echelons -- or link up the top party echelons with the field, people on the ground. And as you can see in the text, we asked that a report be compiled about the justifications and ways in which these would be linked up, which once again meant that practical requirements were needed, should have been met, rather than political ideals. So the practical side was justified and on that level we had permanent contacts with Croatia, for example, because part of Croatia was already functioning and helping us, and part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina occupied with the SAO Krajinas from which the Croatian populace had to free whether they wanted to or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can next go to Exhibit P 00048. Can you tell us, please, whether this is a meeting of the Travnik regional community on the 13th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This document indicates that Mr. Boban attended this particular meeting. Can you give us any assistance as to how it was that Mr. Boban came to attend this regional meeting chaired by Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Had the situation been normal, that would have been quite simple and justified, that one of the vice-presidents should attend a meeting of some regional organisation. However, later on it would transpire that that was not by chance, as well as the fact that the regional organisation of Travnik, for instance, was not satisfied with the formulation made by the president of the Main Board or Presidency of the Main Board of Prozor. Whereas we said that a report should be compiled to justify the relevance and linkage and communication, here it says that the Travnik regional community will stand by the conclusions it has already made. That means they'd already made their conclusions and we, as the higher up level, had to listen to them, especially I myself. And this would lead to a series of problems, and the president of that Travnik region asked me to expound on my behaviour, to explain my behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before you get to that, sir, would you look, so the courtroom can see -- can I direct your attention to paragraph 3 under "Decisions." Were you called to task about some position or action you'd taken around this time, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, let me say first of all that we tried to be as cultivated as possible and to see whether that Travnik initiative should be assessed, evaluated, steered, or whatever. Then he says that they weren't satisfied with that and that he thought my conduct was unacceptable. Okay. That's on a personal level, and you have to understand that. Those were turbulent times. Everybody thought himself to be a leader. Although they didn't win any elections, that's how they behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me correct you, sir. This isn't Mr. Kordic's personal letter. Aren't these the records of a meeting of the Travnik regional community, where it says, "We call on President Stjepan Kljuic to explain his behaviour"? This meeting that Mr. Boban also attended.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Excellent, fine. That's what they wanted, but I didn't have the obligation to comply. Everybody was well aware of political hierarchy. I was a member of the state Presidency and a member of the HDZ with full legitimacy. The fact that somebody didn't like me, well, I told them later on, How can Stjepan Kljuic be replaced? You have to act by the statute and you have to have one more vote on your side, and then if they replace me they'd have to find somebody to replace me with. And that some ambitious young man tried to do this -- I tried to talk to him, but he was behaving in this aggressive manner -- well, that's the result of something that was later seen in its true light, its true colours. He didn't -- I don't believe he had Boban's support at that time, but perhaps he did, but that's their problem. I didn't find it necessary either to change my positions for Travnik or him or to apologise in any way for my behaviour. At Prozor, at the political rally there, I said that this proposal for the regional association should not be rejected but that it should be analysed and looked into, and I gained support from the Main Board. Now, the fact that he says this, that the Travnik community did not agree that its firm conclusions be respected, that's his problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'll look next at paragraph, (h). There are some paragraphs that have letters. If you can find item (h), which the document says, "We demand that the Presidency begin to exploit the fact that BiH is already a partly partitioned country and take a clear stand as to what needs to be done in the new situation." Did you have an understanding as what was being said that BiH by August of 1991 was already "a partly partitioned country"?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, of course the situation was very difficult, but the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina had still not been destroyed. It was exposed to different crises, the aggressive behaviour of the JNA being foremost among them, and the Serbian democratic community which armed the Serbs first on the territory of the whole state and then tried to establish its own administration and to put a stop to life in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you understand, sir, how Mr. Boban and Mr. Kordic, and perhaps others, were demanding that this situation be exploited? How should it be exploited and to what end?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honours, but we have an improper question here. If we see that before that Mr. Kljuic gave the answer and said that he wasn't sure that Boban was with him but perhaps he was, so this present question asked by the Prosecutor somehow distorts Mr. Kljuic's answer and puts words into his mouth, that he said that it was Mr. Boban who stood behind these conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the witness would like to look at the last page of the document and see who the chairpersons at this meeting were once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe the chairpersons of this meeting were Mate Boban, Udovicic and Kordic. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell me how -- what demands were being made that this situation that the country was already partly partitioned should be exploited? What did you know or understand by that? This is directed at you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, I must tell you that this was not a serious request, and I'll tell you why. It's easy to sit in a small town and speak big words. At that time, we were fighting for the Territorial Defence. You know or should know that in the meantime, a year before this, weapons had been confiscated from the Bosnia-Herzegovina Territorial Defence rendering it completely incapable of defending itself from the Serbian aggression. A similar thing happened in Croatia and Croatia paid dearly for it. Only the Slovenian communists did not give up the weapons of their Territorial Defence which is why the war to liberate Slovenia from the JNA lasted a very short [Realtime transcript read in error "long"] time. We were doing a lot to prevent a public conflict, an open conflict, because the JNA and the Serb officers of the KOS were causing incidents. They were transporting weapons. How? They would have a truckload of weapons covered with a layer of bananas. Our policemen often lacked the strength to check this and stop such a convoy or send it back.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: So it is only a matter of translation that I believe it is lines 16 and 17, I believe your statement was not translated properly, because it says that the Slovenian communists did not give up the weapons of the Territorial Defence, which is why the war to liberate Slovenia from the JNA lasted a long time. I believe, of course, the proper interpretation should be that it did not last a long time, if I'm not mistaken. So it's only a question of mine, and I believe it could be easily verified. And taking the floor now, I would like to apologise to the interpreters for when last time I did not actually follow the interpretations properly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you respond to any of the demands being made by the Travnik regional community at this time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was satisfied by the way it was treated at the sessions of the Main Board and the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you look next, please, at Exhibit P 00050. And can you tell us, this is an action -- the minutes of a meeting of the Presidency on the 23rd of August, 1991. Is that correct, sir, of the party?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall whether you were present at this time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Of course. I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was this the action proposed in this document, the creation of these additional regional organisations, was that pursued or implemented following this document?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: These were instructions. That's what should have been done, but it wasn't done for objective and sometimes subjective reasons. By your leave, I'll explain the meaning of these regions to you. In Sarajevo, we were cut off from many of the municipalities inhabited by Croats, or where the Croats were in power. There was no chance for us to regularly send our party materials, especially as there were incidents, for example, where a JNA officer walked into one of our offices in the municipality and took away our fax machine. On the other hand, this creation of regions did not imply any territorial pretensions, because there are municipalities listed here where there are not even 5 per cent of the Croats. But for those 5 per cent who were there, it was important for them to have links with places where there were more Croats. For our people, it was important for them to be grouped together. There were some municipalities where the Croats were not in the majority. They didn't even amount to 40 per cent. But on the right hand and left hand edges of the municipality there would be a compact Croatian milieu. Whether because of administrative divisions in the old Yugoslavia or the new Yugoslavia, that's immaterial. But these people were forced to cooperate, and it was easier for us because we would send things on to the community and then it would distribute the materials further. So this was a normal situation even had there not been a threat of war. Even under peacetime conditions, such regionalisation in terms of the party organisation would have been logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the second paragraph of the introductory portion, it says -- it makes reference that this is a "Prerequisite for the creation of the political and territorial linking of the Croatian people for which purpose special programmes will have to be drawn up." In what way was this a prerequisite for further political and territorial linking up?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it's quite normal, in a situation where everything is divided on an ethnic basis, that the Croats should -- should solve their problems together. This division was a party division. It was important to list all the people, where they lived, where they worked. Many people stopped working at this time. If someone had been working in a Serb-controlled company, they would be out of a job now. Or if as a citizen they were living in surroundings where they were inferior, anybody could open their door, walk into their house, take away their cow and so on. So this was normal for people to join together, but there could be no territorial pretensions here. In the Sarajevo region, for example, in 12 municipalities nowhere except in Ilidza were there more than 20 per cent Croats. In some municipalities there were 2 per cent, 3 per cent, 10, 8 per cent in the centre. So how could you, if that's what you're asking me -- let me tell you right away: How could you have any territorial pretensions if out of 12 municipalities perhaps 5 per cent of the overall population were Croats?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'll next look at Exhibit P 00052. These appear to be minutes of the meeting of the Presidency of the HDZ BiH on the 26th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In item number 6, not -- under "Conclusions," item number 6, it says, "The proposal for the regionalisation of the BiH HDZ municipal boards was adopted and makes an integral part of these conclusions." So can you tell us, sir, at this particular meeting of the Presidency of the party, the proposal to go forward with regional -- with regional organisations was approved; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: This document approves the establishing of regional organisations of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Under item 7, it says that, "President Stjepan Kljuic should attend the next meeting of the Travnik BH HDZ regional organisation in order to solve all misunderstandings that have arisen to date." Did you attend the next meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but the misunderstandings with the president of that region were not removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What misunderstandings were those?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, from our personal relationship to their demands that the Presidency should not manipulate the situation, that the government should do its job. If you sit there and say the government should govern, how can you do that if the Serb ministers in the government were sabotaging the government and their members on the ground were not recognising it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It's easy to put ultimatums like this, but politics is what is possible in a given situation. And you cannot respond in a Draconian manner to every situation. This was impossible. We were on the defensive. There was a war raging in Croatia. Our people were running away to Croatia and helping the struggle of the Croatian people. It was our political task, let me tell you, because the counter-intelligence service of Yugoslavia broadcast a film about Martin Spegelj, the Croatian minister of defence at the time, and they broadcast it 17 times in Belgrade and 12 times in Sarajevo in the space of 24 hours, and we all had to flee our homes because they saw us all as Ustasha. And I spoke out on television and I said it was natural and nobody should be upset by the fact that Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina would help their brethren in Croatia. Of course some citizen lost their respect for me because I said this because they were unaware of the situation in Croatia. You have to know that in Sarajevo the television station was in the hands of Serb nationalists, and as a member of the Presidency and the president of a political party, I did not get even a second of air time. Croats were constantly represented as Ustasha, secessionists, separatists, and so on. Even my civic image and my Bosnian-Herzegovinian patriotism was not enough to counter this. On the other hand --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... look at Exhibit 00056. Can you look at this organisational chart, sir, for the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina and on the first page, which indicates for the period 1991, 1992, as far as you're familiar with it, does that indicate -- is that an accurate representation of the structure of the party at that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the bottom of the page, there is a reference to the HDZ Security Council, and it says "Crisis Staff as of 18 September, 1991." Can you tell us when this body was formed? Not the Crisis Staff as of 18 September, but when was the HDZ Security Council formed?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: As you were able to see in previous minutes, various commissions were established within the HDZ. One was for health. Another was for culture. A third was for the economy. A fourth was for security. In the security commission, all those officials of the state administration who were working in the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior took part. Then the party leadership and some people from the various regions. For example, Filip Evic from Bosanski Samac, Dario Kordic from Travnik, Ivo Lozancic, from Zepce, Bozo Rajic from Kupres, Zeljko Raguz from Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you know, how was it that Mr. Stojic became a member of the Security Council or Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Very simply. Branko Kvesic and Bruno Stojic were our officials within the Ministry of Police, just as Jerko Doko was in the Ministry of Defence, or Bozidar Skravan in the Ministry of Communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what position Mr. Stojic held in the police organisation at that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think the minister had six assistants of various orientations. We had two assistants. One was for state security - that was Branko Kvesic - and another for finance, I think, and that was Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can go now to Exhibit P 00058.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This document is titled "Conclusions of the BH HDZ Security Council meeting held on 18 September, 1991." And I suppose I should ask you, sir, before we leave all these documents, if you look at the last page of the Croatian language version, does that bear your signature?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In paragraph 1 of this document, it indicates that the body that had been called up to that point the Security Council shall from now on be called the Crisis Staff of the BH HDZ. Do you recall any particular reason for changing the name to Crisis Staff at this time in mid-September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It was simply the fashion in Yugoslavia. Bosnia and Herzegovina had its Crisis Staff in the Presidency and the government. The SDA had the same. The SDS did. So why shouldn't we Croats have our own Crisis Staff as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the third paragraph of section 1, it says: "The Crisis Staff shall start working immediately and shall be in charge of the entire system of the defence of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and ensure the acquisition of weapons." Can you tell the Judges what actions were taken during this time to acquire weapons on behalf of the HDZ BiH?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: First of all, it was justified to try and arm the people. All the more so as the Serbs were already heavily armed, and they didn't buy the weapons, they were given them for free. And also a part of the Muslims were armed, especially in Eastern Bosnia.
