So it would have been politically irresponsible and humanly very wrong if, as the president of the Croatian Democratic Union at the time, I had kept silent and simply watched our people being killed in many places.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you to justify the position, but my question is can you describe to the Judges what actions were taken to actually put this into effect? What did you or people working at your direction do to acquire weapons?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Excellent. At that time a large number of Croats from the diaspora wanted to come home and defend Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian people. As the state was blocked, the Territorial Defence was still under the administration of the Yugoslav People's Army, and the retired generals were there. The army had by then cleansed all the Croatian cadres. They had purged them so that only Serbs and Montenegrins were left for the most part, and on the 24th of December, 1991, this was confirmed when Generals Kadijevic and Adzic came to negotiate, and they had 12 Montenegrin generals and one Slovenian admiral. We were duty bound to try and arm the people, and for us it was easier. Because we didn't have any personal contacts, we did this through Zagreb because Zagreb already had open lines through Europe for obtaining weapons because Croatia was bleeding at the time. As the political president and a politician coming from a civil background, I couldn't get involved in this because I didn't know anything about it, but I tasked two of my members, in cooperation with Zagreb, to try and obtain weapons. These were Mate Boban and Iko Stanic. Of course they had other assistance, and that's how it went. So that a part of the Croatian people, the homogenous part, when the war broke out were already armed to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What do you mean the homogenous part was already armed? Which homogenous part of what?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Those were areas in Posavina, Central Bosnia, and Western Herzegovina. When we say they were armed, it was all very little in comparison with the JNA and the Chetniks, but for us citizens of Sarajevo who had nothing, it seemed to be an imposing quantity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But these areas of the Posavina, Central Bosnia, and Western Herzegovina, these were homogenous in what way? According to you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: In Western Herzegovina, they were nationally homogenous, and these were other two -- the other two areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina where the Croats were most grouped together. I told you that the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina are spread from Neum to Brcko, but in some places, such as in the Bihac region, there are very few of us. There are quite a lot of us in Central Bosnia, and in the Posavina area we used to be the most numerous people in five or six municipalities and it was quite normal for people there to defend their own homes, all the more so as especially in Posavina they were it exposed to the fiercest Chetnik aggression because they were in the way of the corridor towards Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we finish for this evening if I could direct your attention, please, to paragraph 11 of the conclusions. By this paragraph apparently something called the Commission for Cantonisation was established. Can you tell us, what was the Commission for Cantonisation and what its mandate was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It was advisory. There were several university professors in this commission from various academic disciplines and of various educational backgrounds. The Serbs at that time were not proposing the break-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina but its cantonisation, referring to examples in Switzerland and so on, but they were still not producing maps because you have to know that the position of the Serbs at this time was such that they practically controlled 70 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas only 31 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina belonged to them. That's the number of municipalities where they were in the majority. Also, this was a backwood area with few towns. The Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina are not so much an urban population. They are more of a rural population. However, their ambitions far outstripped what would belong to them according to some kind of principle of division of the population. That's why they aspired to take certain regions and part of, conditionally speaking, Croatian, in quotation mark, areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the end of the paragraph -- and I'm sorry to interrupt you, but when the translation stops, Mr. Kljuic seems to take that as a signal to keep talking. I apologise to the interpreters. At the end of that paragraph, sir, after listing the members of this commission, it says, "The commission shall deliver a proposal for cantonisation to the Presidency by 22 September, 1991." Can you tell us, were any maps or proposals -- a moment ago you mentioned maps. Were any proposals presented to the Presidency by the cantonisation commission as of 22 September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Kovacic, quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really hate to interrupt. My colleague has already raised a similar objection. We have now come for the first time to a relatively relevant topic, and the Prosecutor is simply interrupting the witness. This is the first time I've heard something that is directly relevant to this case, and now the Prosecutor is not allowing the witness to finish his response. I don't know why then the purpose of all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am speaking in very specific terms, trying to help you see the situation as it really was. The Commission for Cantonisation, the Serbs had such a commission in the SDS, and the Muslims in the SDA. These were commissions composed of eminent experts, including demographers and historians. They were supposed to sit down and then the commissions were supposed to harmonise their positions and see what belonged to whom. Of course if there's a bridge on a river somewhere, you will add a part where there is a road and not a part where there isn't a road. This cantonisation was not supposed to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina but to create a new administrative organisation. Nobody was saying at that time that Bosnia and Herzegovina would no longer exist, but the administrative organisation was supposed to be changed and these experts were supposed to make proposals about these cantons because all the previous administrative units, whatever they were called before, municipalities, counties or whatever, were now to become cantons. However, this work never finished and it was later to be transformed into its very opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a precision, please. You said that the Serbs also had the same type of commission but those Commissions for Cantonisation, they were put in place but pursuant to an order, a directive, a written text, or on the basis of initiatives that were purely local and political, on the part of political parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This was from the top of the political parties as a result of the talks of the presidents, the delegations, and the public opinion of the time. For example, to put it very simply, in an article it said why should we argue? Why should we fight? Let's make a cantonisation of the kind that exists in Switzerland and there will be peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was nobody who did not want to support that at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to stop there for this evening. It's a little past 7.00. Sir, you're going to come back for the proceedings tomorrow morning at 9.00. Between now and then you are not to contact either members of the Prosecution or any of the Defence counsel. Before rising, the Judges would like to turn to Ms. -- to Counsel Jonjic. Mr. Jonjic, we've been informed by the Registry that in the course of the afternoon the appointment of a new counsel to take your place will be -- will go ahead, and he will take up his offices as of his tomorrow, duties as of tomorrow. I would like to inform you of that. On behalf of myself and my other three colleagues, I would like to extend our gratitude to you for the work you've done date for Mr. Coric. We hope to see you back, perhaps in other circumstances, and I would like to thank you once again for the work you have done so far. Having said that, it is now four minutes past 7.00. Unless Mr. Jonjic wishes to take the floor -- now you don't. We can adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I be allowed to say something? Although I haven't been given the go-ahead from the rest of the Defence counsel, from our joint discussions I know that I can speak on their name to thank him for our two years of cooperation and the highly professional work that Tomislav Jonjic has done, and to say that we're very sorry to see him go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, it is now five minutes past 7.00. The meeting is adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of June, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
